Warm-Up: What Does a Digit Mean?

Before we look at binary, let's remind ourselves what a digit is actually worth in a number you already know.

Worked example: 372

100s10s1s
372

The 3 is worth 300, because it sits in the 100s column. The 7 is worth 70. The 2 is worth 2.

Move a digit one column to the left and its value multiplies by 10. That is what place value means.

steps.label: Binary Place Value
steps.content:
Binary Place Value

Denary uses columns worth 100, 10 and 1, each one 10 times the column to its right. Binary works the same way, just with a different multiplier.

  • Every binary column is worth double the column to its right.
  • The columns we will use are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
  • Eight columns like this is called an 8-bit number, or one byte.
  • A column with a 1 in it counts toward the total. A column with a 0 in it does not.
1286432168421
10110100

This example has 1s in the 128, 32, 16 and 4 columns. We will add those up properly in a moment.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • What are the only two digits allowed in binary?
  • What is the value of the leftmost column in an 8-bit number?
  • Do you add up the columns with a 1 in them, or the columns with a 0 in them?
  • What is another word for a single binary digit?
